issues.legal_issue: An unexplained and inordinate delay in seeking special leave is not condoned merely because a later decision enhanced compensation for comparable land.
material_facts: The petitions for special leave were filed more than three years after the High Court’s judgment and were delayed by approximately three years.
The Court was not satisfied that the petitioners had shown sufficient cause for the delay, even after they were given an opportunity to provide further affidavits.
The petitioners relied on later decisions that had enhanced compensation for adjacent land.
issues.conclusion: The delay was not condoned, and the petitions were dismissed as time-barred.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits condonation only where sufficient cause is shown. The later enhancement of compensation in Paltu Singh v. State of Haryana and Nand Kishore v. State of Haryana did not itself constitute sufficient cause for the delay.

rule.if: special_leave_petition and filing_after_limitation_deadline and delay_lacks_sufficient_cause and later_comparable_compensation_increase

predicates.special_leave_petition: The proceeding is a petition seeking special leave to appeal.
predicates.filing_after_limitation_deadline: The petition was filed after the applicable filing deadline.
predicates.delay_lacks_sufficient_cause: The applicant did not establish a sufficient explanation for the delay.
predicates.later_comparable_compensation_increase: A later decision awarded higher compensation for comparable land.

issues.definition: When a special leave petition is filed late without sufficient explanation, a later increase in compensation for comparable land does not prevent the delay from being left uncondoned.

issues.legal_issue: A final land-acquisition compensation award cannot be reopened through redetermination where the applicant had already sought a reference to the civil court.
material_facts: The applicants had sought references under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and received enhanced compensation from the civil court and the High Court.
The High Court’s judgment had become final because the applicants did not seek special leave within the applicable period.
The applicants were not the inarticulate and poor landowners for whose benefit section 28A was intended.

Section 28A provides for redetermination by the Collector, subject to its conditions, for persons who had not applied for a section 18 reference; section 25 would benefit an applicant using that redetermination remedy.
issues.conclusion: Section 28A did not apply to the applicants, and there was no other provision for reopening their final award; section 25 did not provide an independent basis to do so.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18, 25 and 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 operate together: section 28A provides a limited redetermination remedy for eligible persons who did not seek a section 18 reference and who apply within the prescribed time, while section 25 may benefit a person proceeding through that remedy. The Act provides no other means to reopen an award that has become final and conclusive.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.final_compensation_award: The compensation award has become final and conclusive.
predicates.applicant_previously_sought_reference: The applicant previously sought a reference to a civil court to determine compensation.

issues.definition: If a compensation proceeding concerns an award that has become final and the applicant previously sought a civil-court reference, the final award is not reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority is not barred from relying on a well-founded limitation defence by general observations discouraging technical pleas against citizens.
material_facts: The applicants relied on observations in Madras Port Trust v. Hymanshu International discouraging public authorities from using limitation pleas to defeat citizens’ claims.
The Court distinguished that case and noted that it had also recognized that a court must uphold a well-founded limitation plea.
The respondent was a public authority, and the petitions were hopelessly late without sufficient cause.
issues.conclusion: The observations in Madras Port Trust did not create a universal rule preventing a public authority from pleading limitation; a well-founded limitation defence had to be upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Madras Port Trust v. Hymanshu International, [1979] 4 SCC 176, expressed a hope that public authorities would act fairly, but did not establish a universal bar on limitation pleas. It recognized that a court must uphold a well-founded plea of limitation.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: The proceeding is a petition seeking special leave to appeal.
predicates.respondent_is_public_authority: The respondent is a government body or other public authority.
predicates.limitation_bar_is_well_founded: The applicable limitation period has expired and the applicant has not established a legally sufficient basis to overcome the bar.

issues.definition: In a special leave proceeding against a public authority, a well-founded limitation bar is upheld.
